title: Throughput Governor: adaptive soft-throttle using sliding-window token accounting for KV-aware microbatching
creator: Aisha Kaplan
description: Problem: At sustained high QPS we observe repeated spikes in GPU memory >90% when KV cache growth and microbatch coalescing coincide. Current admission controller uses a hard headroom cutoff which either underutilizes capacity (conservative) or causes sharp backpressure cascades (aggressive). Goal: introduce a 'Throughput Governor' — a soft-throttle that maintains steady throughput by accounting for token-level memory pressure, per-model KV footprint, and short-term QPS bursts using a sliding-window token accounting mechanism.
design_notes: Core idea: maintain a lightweight sliding window counter per serving slot that accumulates 'in-flight token units' (request.tokens * expected_seq_len) with exponential decay (EWMA-like) to represent near-term memory commitment. The governor emits a continuous admission probability p in [0,1] computed as p = clamp(1 - (estimated_headroom_usage / target_headroom), 0.05, 1.0). Admission decisions are probabilistic for soft-throttling; deterministic floor ensures minimal fairness. KV awareness: each model-version exposes a compact KV_size_estimate; the algorithm inflates the token units by (1 + kv_multiplier * KV_size_estimate) to capture long-lived memory caused by cached KV slices. Hysteresis: two timescales — short (500ms) for burst smoothing, long (10s) to avoid flip-flopping on transient load. Safety fallback: when headroom < 5% trigger emergency shed (hard reject) with priority-based grace for P99-critical calls. Implementation touches: admission controller, telemetry, per-slot state persisted in in-memory ring buffers, config via runtime flags and per-customer policy overrides.
tradeoffs: Pros: smoother throughput, better GPU utilization, fewer cascade backpressure events, KV-aware decisions. Cons: probabilistic admission can increase tail variance for small cohorts; requires accurate KV_size_estimate and tuning of decay constants. Adds CPU overhead per slot (but bounded) and more telemetry to track. Rollout complexity: need careful canarying to avoid broad regressions.
experiments: Spike simulator run 1 (QA env) — baseline vs governor: baseline showed 18% tail OOMs at 95th percentile load; governor reduced OOM events by 92% and increased steady throughput by 12%
Real cluster shadowing (2h) — enabled governor in shadow mode for subset of slots: headroom variance decreased 38%, average microbatch size increased 9% resulting in 7% lower tokens/sec cost estimate

A/B canary (small cohort, 100 instances) — probabilistic admission tuned to floor=0.08: observed slight P95 latency increase (+40ms) for cheap requests but P99 improved overall due to fewer cache-evict jitter events
acceptance_criteria: 1) No increase in customer-visible error rate in canary (<=0.1% relative). 2) Headroom tail (95th) reduction >= 25% in canary. 3) OOMs or emergency hard-rejects reduced or unchanged. 4) Telemetry hooks emit new events: governor_decision, token_window_size, kv_adjusted_units. 5) Feature flag-controlled rollout with ability to revert within 5 minutes.
rollout_plan: 1) Deploy governor in shadow mode across a small SRE-owned fleet for 48h. 2) Tune decay constants and kv_multiplier based on telemetry. 3) Enable probabilistic admission for 5% traffic cohort for 2h, monitor SLOs/dashboards. 4) Gradually increase cohort to 25% then 100% over 3 days if metrics stable. 5) For Dedicated customers, expose policy knob 'governor_mode' with values {off,shadow,soft,strict}.
implementation_tasks: controller: implement sliding-window token accumulator and probabilistic admission API
runtime: add per-model KV_size_estimate annotation and KV multiplier integration
telemetry: add governor_decision, estimated_headroom, token_units metric series
ops: dashboard & alerting update (headroom-95th, governor_rejections, emergency_sheds)
e2e: add integration test with synthetic KV accumulation and burst patterns
